cheatsheet:
**Addresses**
`&x` is where x lives. `int *p = &x;` makes p point at x.

**Following a pointer**
`*p` is the box p points at: read it (`*p + 1`) or change it (`*p = 75;`).

**Changing the caller's variable**
`void refill(int *tank) { *tank = 100; }` called as `refill(&fuel);`, the same reason scanf needs `&`.

**Pointers and arrays**
An array's name is the address of element 0. `p + 1` is the next element. `*(p + i)` is the same as `p[i]`.

**Structs**
`typedef struct { char name[20]; int age; } Crew;` · `pilot.age` on a struct · `c->age` through a pointer (`(*c).age`)

lessons.title: Every box has an address
lessons.concept:
Every variable lives somewhere in memory, at an **address**. `&fuel` gives you that address.

A **pointer** is a variable that holds an address: `int *p = &fuel;` reads "p points at fuel".

Put `*` in front of a pointer to **follow** it: `*p` is the box p points at. You can read it, or change it. Changing `*p` changes `fuel` itself.

predict.prompt: Before you run it: type what it prints.
predict.explain: `*p` is fuel's box. Writing 75 through p changes fuel itself.

lessons.title: Letting a function change your variables
lessons.concept:
Remember that parameters are copies? To let a function change **your** variable, give it the address instead: `refill(&main_tank);`

The function takes a pointer, `void refill(int *tank)`, and writes through it: `*tank = 100;`.

That's exactly why `scanf` needs `&`: you hand it the address so it can fill your variable.

drills.explain: It swapped its copies. Take pointers (`int *a, int *b`), write through them with `*`, and call it with `swap(&x, &y)`.

lessons.title: Walking through arrays with pointers
lessons.concept:
An array's name is the **address of its first element**, so `int *p = readings;` points at `readings[0]`.

`p + 1` points at the **next element** (C knows how big an int is). `*(p + 2)` is the element two along, which is exactly what `p[2]` means.

That's also how arrays reach functions: `int sum(int *arr, int n)` gets the start address, so you also pass how many elements there are.

predict.prompt: Before you run it: type the four numbers it prints.
predict.explain: p starts at element 0. After `p++` it points at element 1, so `p[1]` means element 2.

drills.explain: `a + 1` is the address of the second element.
It jumps two elements at a time: a[0] + a[2] = 1 + 3.

drills.prompt: Add up the elements `arr` points to.
drills.explain: `arr[i]` and `*(arr + i)` mean the same thing.

drills.prompt: Finish `count_above`: return how many of the n numbers are greater than `limit`. `main` reads n, the numbers, then limit.
drills.explain: The pointer works like the array: loop i from 0 to n − 1 and count `arr[i] > limit`. "Greater than" means 5 isn't above 5.

lessons.title: Structures: crew records
lessons.concept:
A **struct** bundles related values into one thing:

`typedef struct { char name[20]; int age; } Crew;`

Now `Crew` is a type. `Crew pilot = {"Mira", 31};` makes one, and `pilot.age` reaches inside with a dot.

Through a pointer, use an arrow: `c->age` (short for `(*c).age`). Pass a pointer when a function should change the record.
